title: Testing: Every Kind, and What They Have in Common
description: Software testing in depth, then testing everywhere else, then the map between them. One six-part frame covers all of it.

subject.topic: Testing as a general practice, in software and outside it
subject.thesis: Every test in every field has the same six parts. A field's characteristic failure is whichever part it habitually leaves unstated.

scope.objective: Survey software testing in depth, survey testing outside code, and map the two onto each other so practices can move between them.
covers: software testing by scope, technique, generation method, and quality attribute
testing practice and workflow, including shift-left and shift-right
regulated and safety-critical testing, including testing of AI systems
testing in statistics, medicine, manufacturing, education, security, and finance
the failure modes shared across every domain
excludes: quantitative claims about which practices produce better outcomes
test management tooling, staffing models, and outsourcing
scope.evidenceBoundary: Public documentation, standards bodies' own descriptions, published papers, and regulator publications, read on 2026-08-16 and 2026-08-17. No tools were installed or exercised. Paywalled standards were not purchased.

originalContributions: The six-part frame, and the claim that a field's characteristic failure is the part it leaves unstated.
A cross-domain translation table mapping software testing vocabulary to its equivalents in other fields.
Five concrete practices software should take from older testing disciplines, with a worked sampling plan.
The diagnostic matrix in section 09, recomputed rather than quoted, and gated by this generator.

limitations: No tools were installed or exercised. Every claim about tool behaviour comes from documentation or published measurement.
Paywalled standards texts were not purchased. Standards contents are described from the publisher's public material or from technical summaries that cite them.
Only one figure in the report is computed here rather than sourced: the diagnostic matrix in section 09.
The translation table, the six-part frame, and the five proposals are arguments, not measurements.
Accessibility automation coverage is reported by sources as 57%, 20-40%, 29%, and 22.6%; these use different denominators and are presented as such.
Secondary sources describe the 2025 Federal Reserve stress test as covering 22 and 31 banks; the Federal Reserve's own publication says 22, and that is the figure used.
Clinical trial participant counts are typical ranges, not rules.
